solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Manifestation of pride to precede fall: land here?

indicators.note: the pride piece comes before the fall piece, as pride goes before a fall

parts.note: putting on airs is a show of pride, so airs are its manifestation
a trip is a stumble or fall

explanation.surface: A twist on the proverb that pride comes before a fall, ending in a question.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb pulls the eye to pride and fall as a moral; they are simply two consecutive pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An airstrip is a runway where an aircraft may come down; the question mark flags the playful phrasing.

clue.text: Shakespearean villain one with a company around him

indicators.note: the company abbreviation is placed so it surrounds the word him

explanation.surface: A villain from Shakespeare surrounded by his entourage.
explanation.walkthrough: Iachimo is the scheming Italian in Cymbeline who deceives Posthumus about Imogen.
explanation.definitionFit: Iachimo is the scheming deceiver of the play Cymbeline, a classic stage villain.

clue.text: Poor feeder, pike's first observed in very British river

parts.note: so means very, as in so good

indicators.note: the letter is seen inside the words very and British, so it is placed within them
only the opening letter of the word pike is taken

parts.note: the Itchen is a river in Hampshire, England

explanation.surface: An angler spots a pike in a very British river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Itchen is a chalk-stream river flowing through Winchester and Southampton.
explanation.definitionFit: A soup kitchen is a charity serving free meals, so it feeds the poor.

clue.text: Revolver found by soldiers climbing rocky peak

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means the soldiers' letters are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: OR stands for Other Ranks, soldiers who are not officers
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A gun discovered by troops scaling a crag.
explanation.walkthrough: Revolver suggests a pistol, but it is anything that turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the spinning part of a machine or helicopter, so it literally revolves.

clue.text: Model, one sure to drop dead, refused ecstasy

parts.note: a para, a paratrooper, is bound to drop from an aircraft

indicators.note: the dead word turned down the drug, so that letter is removed

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A model, doomed to keel over, says no to drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop dead' reads as one phrase but splits: drop belongs to the paratrooper, dead is the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a perfect example, someone held up as a model to copy.

clue.text: Beetle small with base shortened

indicators.note: the word for base loses its final letter, being cut short

explanation.surface: A beetle described as tiny, with a stunted base.
explanation.definitionFit: A weevil is a small beetle with a long snout that infests grain.

clue.text: Battle without end to save revolutionary work in sport

indicators.note: the battle keeps the work safe inside it
the battle's name loses its last letter
turned round, so the work's letters run backwards

parts.note: op, short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A war without end holding a revolutionary work, set in a sporting context.
explanation.walkthrough: Water polo is a team ball game played in a swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Water polo is a competitive team game played in a pool, so a sport.

clue.text: Muse having to leave for day

indicators.note: the word to departs from the Muse's name

parts.note: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry

explanation.surface: A Muse is obliged to quit for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having to leave' reads as being obliged to go; it is the word to that leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In my day' means in my era, so day here is a period of time.

clue.text: Sounding bell after time gives hint

indicators.note: the answer is what comes after the time letter in the bell word

parts.note: a ringing small bell is tinkling

explanation.surface: A ringing bell after some time gives a clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The bell word is time plus the answer, so the answer is what follows time in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkling is a slight suggestion or vague notion, a hint of something.

clue.text: A change of course we hear follows token response to strike

indicators.note: the sound piece comes after the token

parts.note: a counter is a token used in games

indicators.note: the phrase is heard, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a tack is a change of direction in sailing, so this is a tack

explanation.surface: A sailing manoeuvre follows some sort of token reply to a strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A tack' said aloud matches 'attack'.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterattack is a retaliatory assault made in reply to an enemy's blow.

clue.text: Watch insect here shedding wings

parts.note: a tick, a small bloodsucking creature (loosely an insect)

indicators.note: the word here loses its outer letters, its wings

explanation.surface: Observe the bug here as it drops its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: Ticker is slang for a watch, or for the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticker is informal for a watch, from the sound its mechanism makes.

clue.text: Booze keeps shrew mad for musical man

indicators.note: the spirit holds the jumbled letters within it
the word shrew is driven crazy, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Drink keeps a scolding woman furious, a nod to The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.walkthrough: George Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue and Porgy and Bess.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was an American composer of songs and musicals.

clue.text: Dealer carrying a book drove to meet tribe

indicators.note: the tribe joins on after the first part
the herd holds the next letters inside it

parts.note: a drove is a herd of animals being driven
Asher is one of the twelve tribes of Israel

explanation.surface: A trader with a book drove off to meet a tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for a herd.
explanation.definitionFit: A haberdasher is a trader in sewing goods, ribbons and buttons, so a kind of dealer.

clue.text: Left mate on roundabout, playing with a slide?

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, the slide itself; this phrase describes playing in that style

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

indicators.note: the letters are sent round about, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone left their friend on a fairground ride, playing on a slide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roundabout' suggests a playground, as does slide; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Portamento is a smooth glide in pitch from one note to another in singing or string playing.

clue.text: One sort guzzling another quiet drink

indicators.note: the first sort swallows the others inside it

parts.note: a make is a brand or sort
ilk is another word for sort

explanation.surface: One kind of person gulping down another quiet drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' leans on the earlier sort: it means another word for sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A milkshake is a cold beverage of milk whisked with flavouring or ice cream.

clue.text: What's said when claiming many lands

definitions.meaning: '...!' or '... I' is a children's cry to claim something
... as a verb means catches or secures

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings of one word; 'bags I' is British schoolyard slang for calling dibs.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as a claiming cry, as an informal plenty, and as a verb for capturing.

clue.text: Nurse in warm bath regularly

indicators.note: every other letter of the phrase is taken at a regular interval

explanation.surface: A nurse bathing someone in warm water at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: An amah is a nursemaid in parts of Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Amah is a word for a nursemaid or wet nurse in South and East Asia.

clue.text: Second heron bothered smaller waterbird

indicators.note: the heron is upset, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A second heron is disturbed by a lesser water bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second heron' reads as another heron; second is a brief moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The moorhen is a modest-sized rail of ponds, smaller than the heron in the clue.

clue.text: Print from plate and table next to burning house

indicators.note: the table piece sits beside the others

parts.note: a graph is a chart, like a table of data

explanation.surface: Printing from a plate, with a table beside a house on fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A lithograph is an image printed from a flat stone or metal plate treated with grease and water.

clue.text: Best to clothe dancing nude looking firm

indicators.note: the best word wraps round the dancer, dressing it
the word nude moves about, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Better to cover up the naked dancer, who looks in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a phrasal adjective; firm here means muscular, not resolute.
explanation.definitionFit: Toned up describes a body made taut and fit by exercise.

clue.text: Drunk as a skunk perhaps draped round looker?

indicators.note: the skunk word hangs around the looker, enclosing it

parts.note: pied means black and white, like a skunk

explanation.surface: Drunk as a skunk, hung around somebody attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk as a skunk' is a stock phrase, but only drunk is the definition; the skunk is for its colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Pie-eyed is informal for intoxicated, like someone very much the worse for wear.

clue.text: Leaving child constitutes misconduct

explanation.surface: A child walking out counts as bad behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Goings-on are dubious or improper happenings, a coy word for bad behaviour.

clue.text: Harvester in back-breaking exercise?

indicators.note: the exercise splits the back word open, lying inside it

explanation.surface: Farm labour as back-breaking exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-breaking' reads as one word for hard work; it splits into back and breaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A reaper is a person or machine that cuts and gathers crops.

clue.text: One with thick skin runs in circle to corral horse

indicators.note: the pieces pen the horse inside them

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
H is slang for heroin, known as horse

explanation.surface: Someone runs in a ring to round up a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is drug slang for heroin, whose abbreviation is H.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros has famously tough hide; thick-skinned also means insensitive.

clue.text: Self-important as Hercules on a bender?

definitions.meaning: the straight reading: haughty and arrogant
the strongman when drunk would be intoxicated and strong at once

explanation.surface: A pompous figure compared with the legendary strongman on a drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase splits into drunk plus strong, exactly what Hercules on a binge would be.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes an arrogant person who acts superior to others.

clue.text: Sound cut short in viscous liquid

indicators.note: the word loses its final letter

parts.note: sound means good, in good condition

explanation.surface: A noise clipped within a thick fluid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' suggests noise, but it is the adjective, as in sound health.
explanation.definitionFit: Goo is a sticky, thick substance, a gloopy fluid.

clue.text: Liner in Korean city's sound

indicators.note: the city's name is said, giving a word of the same pronunciation

explanation.surface: An ocean liner in the waters off a Korean city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liner' suggests a ship, but it is something lining a shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: An insole is the inner lining layer of a shoe.

clue.text: Bulge in pants Mrs Grundy hides?

indicators.note: the prude conceals the rubbish within

parts.note: Mrs Grundy, from an 18th-century play, is the byword for a narrow-minded prude
pants is British slang for rubbish, as is rot

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of a bulge in trousers that a prim lady covers up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is British slang for nonsense, not trousers here.
explanation.definitionFit: To protrude is to stick out, and so to bulge outward.
